rv.q: But "Suffs," which tells the story of the final push to achieve the 19th Amendment giving women the right to vote in 1920, does just that with a singular vision and a collective collaboration that is smart, inspiring and thoroughly entertaining.
It’s genuinely tuneful and effective at organizing strong characters around a complex series of events.
Taub has written a musical that feels like a textbook come to life — which is both its strength and its weakness. The show is educational in the best sense, but it's also sometimes airless.

Forget the world stage, what about Broadway? This is the route that Hillary Clinton has taken as the co-producer, with Malala Yousafzai, of Suffs, a thundering new musical by the singer and composer Shaina Taub about the American women’s suffrage movement.
"Suffs" on Broadway is vastly improved.
Suffs largely succeeds in showcasing the accomplishments of its creators and performers.
But, in the end, “Suffs” does what all of the best Broadway musicals do: it humanizes and empowers, and it entertains and moves an audience.
Shaina Taub's musical about the women's suffrage movement is an ambitious and often stirring work that brings passion and intelligence to an important chapter in American history.
What “Suffs” does capture is the excitement and urgency of being swept up in the fight for a just cause, and discovering yourself and your peers in the process.
Still, while never less than likable, “Suffs” comes short of being riveting.
But this unapologetic love letter to those who risked life and limb to get women a seat at the table is also heart-tugging, vibrant and charming.
Aside from all that, dramatically speaking, it’s just that good!
“Suffs” entertains because Taub makes her show all about the women, and she makes those women committed but very flawed individuals.
“Suffs” could use some rethinking, but it deserves an audience past its current run.
Winning the vote feels inevitable throughout, so without deep emotional stakes to drive the story, Suffs can feel plodding as it hits the historical beats.
Suffs is a flawed work that fails to emotionally grab, but succeeds as a fresh reminder of the necessity and power of sustained political action.
Unfortunately, there is too much plotting to sustain the show, which has enough to shoulder to make the point that the battle for equality in all arenas is never a fait accompli.
That’s a fitting message — progress comes only through perseverance — for a remarkable musical that educates and entertains.
Suffs reminds us that, as important as individual convictions and rights are, when we can agree on enough to unite side-by-side, we can change the world.
Indeed, Taub has a unique and accomplished gift for melody and lyrics that makes you want to hear more of her work.
Taub (book, lyrics and music) has taken this weighty subject, one full of passion, sadness and personal sacrifice, and has fashioned a theater work that deftly balances history and entertainment.
Suffs is the musical I needed as a little girl and the musical we need today.
Suffs is a winner, with a wonderful mixture of earnest storytelling, humor, and heart.
In case the fire in your belly has gone out, “Suffs” will throw some coal on it.
